Plus: 57 "powerful" nukes | Wednesday, August 26, 2026
 
View in browser
 
PRESENTED BY LOCKHEED MARTIN
 
Axios Future of Defense
By Colin Demarest · Aug 26, 2026

Good morning. September nears.

  • We're growing the Future of Defense team. Know business, capital and appropriations? Want to write smartly? How about briefly? Apply here.

💵 Situational awareness: Mara raised $7 million. The round was led by Khosla Ventures. The money will be used to build Spike, an FPV drone countermeasure described as "fully attritable from the sensors to the interceptors."

Serving: North Korean nukes, air defense as a service and Qatar's multibillion-dollar KC-46A buy.

Today's newsletter is 1,743 words, a 6.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Fort Bragg field trip
 

A Ford F-250, made smart and outfitted with counter-drone and counter-mine gear. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios
 

FORT BRAGG, North Carolina — The scrubby, scorching-hot hills of Range 63 bustled last week with soldiers and contractors. Some nursed cans of Monster. Some rocked sunglasses and sun shirts. Some handled shotgun magazines.

  • A futuristic Ford F-250 was posted at one end of the range. Atop sat a 12-gauge turret, dubbed Edda, that shredded two targets as they flew overhead.
  • A small shipping container labeled "Bee Hive" was parked at the other end. It brimmed with Bumblebee V2 drones, which zipped toward the horizon one after the other.
  • In the middle, a crew with Safe Pro AI pored over aerial imagery and algorithms to identify hidden mines.
  • And somewhere farther off, another F-250 finessed a slurry line charge into place. Its detonation, seen and felt, hurled into the air smoke and dust.

The big picture: This hourslong jam session was part of Sandhills 2.0, an ongoing experiment meant to remove U.S. troops from some of the bloodiest battlefield tasks, like breaching.

  • More broadly, the tinkering shows just how deeply lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war have penetrated parts of the Army.
Detonation aftermath, as seen from a berm at Range 63. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios

What they're saying: "It's a new era of warfare," Col. Jeff Burges, commander of the 20th Engineer Brigade, told reporters at the range.

  • The brigade manages Sandhills and is assigned to the XVIII Airborne Corps.
  • "Gone are the days of a soldier running with a grapnel hook," Burges said. "As we think through the next evolution, it's attacking the enemy with that attritable, autonomous mass."

Zoom in: Texas-based 9 Mothers furnished the drone countermeasure, which used a Genesis Arms shotgun. (9 Mothers is working on a belt-fed system, designed in-house, according to CEO Russell Smith.) California-based Perennial Autonomy provided the drones, dozens of which can be stacked inside the hive. Maryland-based Forterra ruggedized the F-250s and made them smart, capable of self-driving, sensing and communicating.

  • "The Army is super self-aware that it needs to stop delivering yesterday's technology tomorrow," Col. Tom Monaghan, the director of the Joint Innovation Outpost, told reporters.
  • "That's why they're doing these types of on-site experiments with soldiers, with vendors, with acquisition professionals," he said.
  • "Something that's good enough 100% tomorrow isn't good if we're leaving today."
Drones stacked inside the "Bee Hive." The container can be quickly hauled away. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios

Zoom out: Battlefields are increasingly mechanized. In Eastern Europe, autonomous and uncrewed tech is being used to assault trenches, evacuate the wounded, shuttle supplies and spy on positions far afield.

  • Militaries and weapons makers are scrambling to keep up. Commercially available products with widely available, cheap parts are having a moment.
  • "I think there's a strong argument to be made that in order to really proliferate these UGVs at scale ... biasing toward a vehicle that looks like this and has a supply chain like this and has a maintenance tail like this is a good thing to do," Forterra's Phil Cotter told reporters while standing beside an F-250.

What we're watching: Where and how the Army strikes a balance between tradition, like a multimillion-dollar assault breacher vehicle, and novelty, like an armed, self-navigating pickup truck.

2. Rolls-Royce's expansion
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Rolls-Royce will this week mark the completion of a $1 billion investment in Indiana, where the company has expanded and renovated its manufacturing, assembly and test facilities.

The big picture: The overhaul competitively positions Rolls-Royce amid wartime-production messaging from the Pentagon and a growing portfolio of projects, including propulsion for the Army's MV-75, the Air Force's B-52J and the Navy's MQ-25A.

  • "If you go back to 2014, we knew that we were at an inflection point. We had aging facilities, some dating back to World War II," Adam Riddle, president of Rolls-Royce Defense, told me.
  • "We didn't have the productivity or the efficiency that we needed, and we knew we had to make a decision," he said. "Are we going to manage a slow decline, or are we going to compete for the future?"

Driving the news: Hundreds of people are expected to attend a ribbon-cutting tomorrow. Expected speakers include Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, Adjutant General Maj. Gen. Lawrence Muennich and Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett.

Follow the money: The $1 billion investment can be divided into two batches:

  1. $600 million spent modernizing advanced manufacturing, which wrapped in 2021;
  2. And $400 million spent on new engine-testing infrastructure.

Context: The company has pumped out 14,000-plus engines at its Indianapolis campus since 2001. About half can be traced back to the AE line, seen in the Lockheed Martin C-130J and the Bell-Boeing V-22, among others.

The bottom line: "We have capacity — right now — to handle increased growth in our core products, increased growth in the programs that we have in development and the programs we think we're going to win," Riddle said.

  • "We can do the tests faster. We're doing it more efficiently."

Go deeper: Rolls-Royce begins MV-75 engine tests in Indiana
 
 
3. North Korean nuke nuance
 

Illustration: Rebecca Zisser/Axios
 

President Trump recently blurted out that North Korea has 57 "very powerful" nuclear weapons.

  • Experts told me that is believable, but is most likely an undercount.

Why it matters: Nuclear arsenals are often spoken of in generalities — round numbers, increases and decreases, confidence levels. Specifics like this, especially from the very top, are rare and raise hackles.

Driving the news: Trump's comment, delivered during a press tour of White House construction projects, came shortly after he ordered military drills with South Korea be pared back.

  • "Should've never allowed it to happen. They should've never allowed it," Trump said of North Korea's nuclear buildup. "If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them."

By the numbers: The public estimates of Pyongyang's stockpile vary.

  • The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute this summer pegged it "around 60 warheads," with "enough fissile material to produce at least 30 more."

What they're saying: The intelligence community "doesn't provide highly specific singular numeric estimates of adversary nuclear forces like this. If Trump heard a number, it was almost certainly a range," Ankit Panda at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told me.

  • "Among the major uncertainties today is how much of North Korea's weapons-useable nuclear material is actually inside useable and missile-mateable nuclear warheads."

What's next: Trump is angling for a meeting this year with North Korea's Kim Jong-un. They last rendezvoused in 2019.

4. ICYMI 1.0: Erik Prince's ADaaS
By Colin Demarest
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Vectus Air Defense Systems launched Friday, led by Blackwater founder Erik Prince and backed by drone-collaboration specialist Swarmer.

Why it matters: The company is taking an unorthodox tack, applying the as-a-service model, often associated with software subscriptions, to overhead defenses like jammers, cannons and interceptors seen on the battlefields of Ukraine and the Middle East.

  • "It's clear that the threat is evolving rapidly, and the demand for a private-sector solution is very strong," Prince said in a statement to Axios.
  • "We need to achieve a drastic reduction in the cost of defense and to enable customers to take the protection of critical assets into their own hands."

The big picture: Much critical infrastructure was designed or built before today's proliferation of cheap, exploding drones. Military bases, data centers, shipping lanes and refineries are being bombarded the world over.

Read the full story.
 
 
5. ICYMI 2.0: Mo money, mo missiles
By Dan Primack and Colin Demarest
 

Illustration: Lazaro Gamio/Axios
 

Castelion, a California-based developer of hypersonic missiles, raised $800 million in Series C equity funding at a $13 billion post-money valuation.

Why it matters: Startups are racing to help fill stockpiles depleted by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

By the numbers: The round was led by JPMorgan's strategic investment group, a16z and Carlyle.

  • Other backers include Lightspeed, Lavrock Ventures, Altimeter, General Catalyst, Interlagos and T. Rowe Price.
  • Castelion also secured $250 million for a revolving credit facility.

The bottom line: "There's a manufacturing renaissance underway," CEO Bryon Hargis said in a statement, "and this round turbocharges American production of Blackbeard."

Go deeper: Castelion's Blackbeard missile will fly on F/A-18
 
 
6. Quick hits
 

A U.S. Air Force KC-46A Pegasus, flown by the 141st Air Refueling Squadron. Photo: Michael Hong/DVIDS
 

🇶🇦 The State Department approved a potential sale of Boeing-made KC-46As and related equipment to Qatar for $4.5 billion.

  • Why it matters: The notification describes Qatar, which last year secured a diet version of Article 5 with the U.S., as "an important force for political stability and economic progress in the Middle East."
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Yes, price tags can change during negotiations. But it's a huge commitment, either way.

🌌 Muon Space raised $250 million. The Series C was led by Eclipse Capital. Other participants included Galvanize, Salesforce Ventures and Woven Capital.

  • Why it matters: "Space infrastructure needs to scale the way cloud infrastructure did," CEO Jonny Dyer said in a statement.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Is space the new drones? (Not bait, I swear.)

🪖 Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief of staff, published his vision for the service, which states that a "secure Western Hemisphere is a prerequisite for joint power projection" and that the "next war will not look like our last."

  • Why it matters: "Gen. LaNeve is releasing his azimuth now because soldiers deserve to know how the Army fights and what's expected of them," Maj. Peter Sulzona, a spokesperson, told me.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Have you read the Wall Street Journal exclusive? Thoughts?

💥 Hanwha Defense USA plans to deliver its first Mobile Tactical Cannon prototype to the Army this fall.

  • Why it matters: It's HDUSA's first major contract with the service — and it's on a speedy schedule. (Hanwha has 2,500-plus K9 howitzers fielded globally.)
  • 💭 My thought bubble: The Army has been exploring M777 replacements for years now. We'll see what sticks.
 
 
7. Check this out
 

The Surveyor-Joint Air-to-Ground Missile combo. Photo: Courtesy of Saildrone
 

Saildrone conducted two Joint Air-to-Ground Missile launches from its Surveyor drone-boat at the Rim of the Pacific exercise this summer.

Why it matters: The hybrid fleet is getting teeth.

Catch up quick: Saildrone and Lockheed Martin, the maker of JAGM, have been collaborating for months.

Zoom out: Dozens of nations, more than 30 surface ships and tens of thousands of personnel participated in RIMPAC this year.
